title: Behavioral Nonprogression in Job Recommendation: From Prediction to Ranking
content: Behavioral interactions inform job recommendation, yet it remains unclear whether predicting nonprogression improves the ranking of alternative vacancies. Using 65.4 million deduplicated OLX interactions, this exploratory offline study evaluates conditional ranking on 12,783 eligible test queries and a separate full-catalog ranking task involving 619,032 users. Histories containing only information available before prediction enter a multilayer perceptron that estimates finite-window nonprogression. Its output weights aggregate candidate histories rather than providing candidate-specific risk probabilities. Matched fixed, shuffled, contextual, and success-only controls distinguish prediction quality from ranking utility. Behavioral histories improve nonprogression prediction over a context-only model in the selected cohort, but personalized-risk fusion does not establish additional ranking value over matched risk controls. Common-reference normalization and target-rank diagnostics characterize this result. In the separate full-catalog task, which uses no predicted source risk, contact-count fusion improves the RP3Beta graph baseline, while popularity, recency, and the fixed degree-recency component of P3 Learning to Rank (P3LTR) remain more accurate. An exploratory REES46 Cosmetics Shop analysis examines personalization using cart-to-purchase interactions. These findings demonstrate the importance of evaluating behavioral prediction and recommendation utility separately, using matched controls to distinguish personalized-risk effects from aggregate interaction evidence.
